category: Control System Toolbox > Modeling, Analysis & Design
description: Creating LTI models in transfer-function, zero-pole-gain, state-space and frequency-response form; time and frequency response analysis; model interconnection and conversion; and classical and state-space controller design.

tools.name: tf
tools.description: Create a transfer-function model from numerator and denominator polynomial coefficients, for continuous or discrete time. It also converts any other LTI model into transfer-function form, and with no arguments creates the Laplace variable s for building models by algebra. Input/output delays and names can be set through name/value pairs.
tools.usage:
sys = tf(num, den)
sys = tf(num, den, Ts)
sys = tf(sys_other)
s = tf('s')
z = tf('z', Ts)
sys = tf(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: num, den
parameters.description: Numerator and denominator coefficients in descending powers; cell arrays for MIMO systems.

parameters.name: Ts
parameters.description: Sample time in seconds; 0 or omitted means continuous, -1 means unspecified.

parameters.name: 'InputDelay' / 'OutputDelay' / 'IODelay'
parameters.description: Time delays in seconds (or samples for discrete models).

parameters.name: 'InputName' / 'OutputName'
parameters.description: Signal names used in plots and when connecting models.

tools.notes: Building models with s = tf('s') is far more readable than coefficient vectors for anything nontrivial.

tools.name: zpk
tools.description: Create a zero-pole-gain model from vectors of zeros, poles and a scalar gain. This factored form is numerically better conditioned than polynomial coefficients and makes the pole and zero locations immediately visible. Use zpk('s') or zpk('z') to build models by algebra in factored form.
tools.usage:
sys = zpk(z, p, k)
sys = zpk(z, p, k, Ts)
sys = zpk(sys_other)
s = zpk('s')
sys = zpk(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: z, p
parameters.description: Zero and pole locations (cell arrays for MIMO).

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: Overall gain.

parameters.name: Ts
parameters.description: Sample time; 0 for continuous time.

parameters.name: 'DisplayFormat'
parameters.description: 'roots' (default), 'frequency' or 'time-constant'.

tools.name: ss
tools.description: Create a state-space model from the A, B, C and D matrices, in continuous or discrete time. State-space is the natural form for MIMO systems, for modern control design (LQR, Kalman, MPC) and for simulation. It also converts any other LTI model into state-space form.
tools.usage:
sys = ss(A, B, C, D)
sys = ss(A, B, C, D, Ts)
sys = ss(sys_other)
sys = ss(___, Name, Value)
[A, B, C, D] = ssdata(sys)

parameters.name: A, B, C, D
parameters.description: State, input, output and feedthrough matrices.

parameters.name: Ts
parameters.description: Sample time; 0 for continuous time.

parameters.name: 'StateName' / 'InputName' / 'OutputName'
parameters.description: Names for states and signals.

parameters.name: 'InputDelay' / 'OutputDelay'
parameters.description: Delays on the signal paths.

tools.name: frd
tools.description: Create a frequency-response data model from measured or computed complex response values at specified frequencies. It lets you analyse and plot experimental measurements with the same functions as analytic models. Use it to compare a measured plant against a model, or as input to model fitting.
tools.usage:
sys = frd(response, frequency)
sys = frd(response, frequency, Ts)
sys = frd(sys_other, frequency)
sys = frd(___, 'FrequencyUnit', unit)

parameters.name: response
parameters.description: Complex frequency-response values (ny-by-nu-by-nf for MIMO).

parameters.name: frequency
parameters.description: Frequency vector.

parameters.name: 'FrequencyUnit'
parameters.description: 'rad/TimeUnit' (default) or 'Hz'.

tools.name: pid
tools.description: Create a PID controller object in parallel form with proportional, integral, derivative and filter coefficients. The object carries its own structure, so functions like pidtune and step understand it directly. Use pidstd for the standard (ISA) form with Ti and Td parameters.
tools.usage:
C = pid(Kp, Ki, Kd)
C = pid(Kp, Ki, Kd, Tf)
C = pid(Kp, Ki, Kd, Tf, Ts)
C = pid(sys)
C = pid(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: Kp, Ki, Kd
parameters.description: Proportional, integral and derivative gains.

parameters.name: Tf
parameters.description: First-order derivative filter time constant.

parameters.name: Ts
parameters.description: Sample time for a discrete controller.

parameters.name: 'IFormula' / 'DFormula'
parameters.description: Discrete integration method: 'ForwardEuler', 'BackwardEuler', 'Trapezoidal'.

tools.name: pidtune
tools.description: Automatically tune a PID controller for a given plant to balance reference tracking and robustness. You can specify the controller type ('P', 'PI', 'PID', 'PIDF', ...) and a target crossover frequency or phase margin. The second output reports the achieved crossover frequency, phase margin and stability.
tools.usage:
C = pidtune(sys, type)
C = pidtune(sys, C0)
C = pidtune(sys, type, wc)
[C, info] = pidtune(___, opts)

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: 'P', 'PI', 'PD', 'PDF', 'PID', 'PIDF', or a pid/pidstd object to match.

parameters.name: wc
parameters.description: Target open-loop crossover frequency in rad/s; higher is faster but less robust.

parameters.name: opts
parameters.description: pidtuneOptions with 'PhaseMargin', 'DesignFocus' ('balanced', 'reference-tracking', 'disturbance-rejection'), 'NumUnstablePoles'.

tools.name: pidTuner
tools.description: Open the PID Tuner app for interactive tuning, with sliders for response time and transient behaviour and live plots of the closed-loop response. It shows step responses, Bode plots and the resulting robustness margins as you drag. Export the tuned controller to the workspace when you are satisfied.
tools.usage:
pidTuner
pidTuner(sys)
pidTuner(sys, type)
pidTuner(sys, C0)

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: Plant model to tune against.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: Controller type string such as 'PI' or 'PIDF'.

parameters.name: C0
parameters.description: An existing pid controller used as the baseline for comparison.

tools.notes: Requires a display. For scripted and repeatable tuning use pidtune.

tools.name: step
tools.description: Compute and plot the unit step response of a dynamic system. With output arguments it returns the response data and time vector instead of plotting, which is what you want in scripts. Several systems can be overlaid in one call for comparison.
tools.usage:
step(sys)
step(sys, Tfinal)
step(sys, t)
step(sys1, sys2, ..., Tfinal)
[y, t] = step(sys)
[y, t, x] = step(sys)

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: Any LTI model (tf, zpk, ss, frd) or an array of models.

parameters.name: Tfinal
parameters.description: End time of the simulation.

parameters.name: t
parameters.description: Explicit time vector (must be uniformly spaced for discrete systems).

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: State trajectories, for state-space models.

tools.name: impulse
tools.description: Compute and plot the impulse response of a dynamic system, which is the inverse Laplace or Z transform of its transfer function. It shows the system's natural modes directly and is the kernel of the convolution that produces any other response. Returns data instead of plotting when output arguments are requested.
tools.usage:
impulse(sys)
impulse(sys, Tfinal)
impulse(sys, t)
[y, t] = impulse(sys)
[y, t, x] = impulse(sys)

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: LTI model.

parameters.name: Tfinal / t
parameters.description: Simulation horizon or explicit time vector.

tools.notes: For a discrete system the impulse applied has amplitude 1/Ts so that the response matches the continuous case.

tools.name: lsim
tools.description: Simulate the response of a dynamic system to an arbitrary input signal defined by a time vector and input samples. Initial conditions can be supplied for state-space models, and an interpolation method chosen for continuous systems. Use it to test controllers against realistic reference and disturbance profiles.
tools.usage:
lsim(sys, u, t)
lsim(sys, u, t, x0)
lsim(sys, u, t, x0, method)
[y, tOut, x] = lsim(___)

parameters.name: u
parameters.description: Input signal samples (one column per input).

parameters.name: t
parameters.description: Uniformly spaced time vector matching u.

parameters.name: x0
parameters.description: Initial state vector for state-space models.

parameters.name: method
parameters.description: 'zoh' or 'foh' interpolation for continuous-time systems.

tools.name: initial
tools.description: Compute the free (unforced) response of a state-space model from a given initial state. It reveals how the system's natural modes decay and is the standard way to check stability and settling from a disturbed state. Only defined for state-space models because it needs explicit states.
tools.usage:
initial(sys, x0)
initial(sys, x0, Tfinal)
initial(sys, x0, t)
[y, t, x] = initial(___)

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: State-space model.

parameters.name: x0
parameters.description: Initial state vector.

parameters.name: Tfinal / t
parameters.description: Simulation horizon or time vector.

tools.name: stepinfo
tools.description: Compute step-response performance metrics: rise time, settling time, overshoot, undershoot, peak value and peak time. Thresholds for rise and settling are configurable. It turns a visual judgement of a step plot into hard numbers you can use as design targets.
tools.usage:
S = stepinfo(sys)
S = stepinfo(y, t)
S = stepinfo(y, t, yfinal)
S = stepinfo(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: yfinal
parameters.description: Steady-state value to use; defaults to the last value of y.

parameters.name: 'RiseTimeLimits'
parameters.description: Two-element fraction vector, default [0.1 0.9].

parameters.name: 'SettlingTimeThreshold'
parameters.description: Fractional band, default 0.02 (2%).

tools.name: bode
tools.description: Plot the Bode magnitude and phase frequency response of a dynamic system on logarithmic frequency axes. With output arguments it returns magnitude, phase and frequency arrays instead of plotting. It is the central tool of classical frequency-domain design.
tools.usage:
bode(sys)
bode(sys, w)
bode(sys1, sys2, ..., w)
[mag, phase, wout] = bode(sys)
[mag, phase, wout, sdmag, sdphase] = bode(sys, w)

parameters.name: w
parameters.description: Frequency vector in rad/TimeUnit, or {wmin, wmax} for a range.

parameters.name: mag, phase
parameters.description: 3-D arrays (ny-by-nu-by-nf); magnitude is absolute, phase in degrees.

tools.notes: The magnitude output is a linear ratio, not dB; convert with 20*log10 and squeeze the singleton dimensions.

tools.name: bodemag
tools.description: Plot only the Bode magnitude response, omitting the phase plot. It is useful when comparing many systems, for filter shaping, and for weighting-function design in robust control. Accepts the same arguments and line-style syntax as bode.
tools.usage:
bodemag(sys)
bodemag(sys, w)
bodemag(sys1, sys2, ..., w)
bodemag(___, plotoptions)

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: One or more LTI models.

parameters.name: w
parameters.description: Frequency vector or {wmin, wmax} range.

parameters.name: plotoptions
parameters.description: A bodeoptions object controlling units, grid and limits.

tools.name: nyquist
tools.description: Plot the Nyquist diagram, the polar trace of the open-loop frequency response over positive and negative frequencies. Encirclements of the -1 point determine closed-loop stability via the Nyquist criterion, which works even for unstable open-loop plants. With outputs it returns the real and imaginary parts.
tools.usage:
nyquist(sys)
nyquist(sys, w)
nyquist(sys1, sys2, ...)
[re, im, wout] = nyquist(sys)

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: LTI model, usually the open-loop transfer function.

parameters.name: w
parameters.description: Frequency vector or range.

tools.name: nichols
tools.description: Plot the Nichols chart, showing open-loop gain in dB against phase in degrees. Overlaying closed-loop magnitude contours with ngrid lets you read off the closed-loop peak gain directly. It is the traditional tool for loop shaping to a resonant-peak specification.
tools.usage:
nichols(sys)
nichols(sys, w)
nichols(sys1, sys2, ...)
[mag, phase, wout] = nichols(sys)

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: Open-loop LTI model.

parameters.name: w
parameters.description: Frequency vector or {wmin, wmax}.

tools.example:
L = tf(20, conv([1 0], [1 4 20]));
nichols(L)
ngrid
title('Nichols chart with closed-loop contours')

tools.name: margin
tools.description: Compute the gain margin, phase margin and their crossover frequencies for an open-loop system. These are the classical robustness measures: how much extra gain or phase lag the loop can tolerate before going unstable. With no output arguments it draws an annotated Bode plot.
tools.usage:
[Gm, Pm, Wcg, Wcp] = margin(sys)
[Gm, Pm, Wcg, Wcp] = margin(mag, phase, w)
margin(sys)

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: Open-loop LTI model.

parameters.name: Gm
parameters.description: Gain margin as an absolute ratio; convert to dB with 20*log10.

parameters.name: Pm
parameters.description: Phase margin in degrees.

parameters.name: Wcg, Wcp
parameters.description: Gain-crossover and phase-crossover frequencies.

tools.notes: allmargin returns every crossing and the delay margin, which matters when there are multiple crossovers.

tools.name: sigma
tools.description: Plot the singular values of a MIMO frequency response, which generalize Bode magnitude to multivariable systems. The largest singular value bounds the worst-case gain over all input directions, and the smallest bounds the best case. It is the main analysis plot for robust and H-infinity control.
tools.usage:
sigma(sys)
sigma(sys, w)
sigma(sys, w, type)
[sv, wout] = sigma(sys)

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: MIMO LTI model.

parameters.name: w
parameters.description: Frequency vector or range.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: 1 for sigma of inv(sys), 2 for I+sys, 3 for I+inv(sys).

tools.name: rlocus
tools.description: Plot the root locus, the trajectories of the closed-loop poles as a scalar feedback gain varies from zero to infinity. It shows directly how gain affects damping, natural frequency and stability. rlocfind lets you click a point on the locus to read off the corresponding gain.
tools.usage:
rlocus(sys)
rlocus(sys, k)
rlocus(sys1, sys2, ...)
[r, k] = rlocus(sys)
[k, poles] = rlocfind(sys)

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: Open-loop LTI model (SISO).

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: Explicit vector of gains to evaluate.

parameters.name: r
parameters.description: Matrix of closed-loop pole locations, one column per gain.

tools.name: pzmap
tools.description: Plot the poles and zeros of a system in the complex plane, with poles as crosses and zeros as circles. For continuous systems stability requires all poles in the left half plane; for discrete systems, inside the unit circle. Use iopzmap to see the pole-zero map of each input-output pair separately.
tools.usage:
pzmap(sys)
pzmap(sys1, sys2, ...)
[p, z] = pzmap(sys)

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: One or more LTI models.

parameters.name: p, z
parameters.description: Pole and zero vectors returned instead of plotting.

tools.name: pole
tools.description: Return the poles of a dynamic system as a column vector. Pole locations determine stability and the character of the natural response. For state-space models the poles are the eigenvalues of the A matrix.
tools.usage:
P = pole(sys)
P = pole(sys, J1, ..., JN)

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: Any LTI model, or an array of models.

parameters.name: J1..JN
parameters.description: Indices selecting an element of a model array.

tools.notes: esort and dsort sort poles by continuous and discrete stability respectively.

tools.name: zero
tools.description: Return the transmission zeros of a dynamic system and optionally the gain. Right-half-plane (nonminimum-phase) zeros limit achievable bandwidth and cause initial undershoot in the step response. For MIMO systems these are the transmission zeros, not the zeros of individual entries.
tools.usage:
Z = zero(sys)
[Z, gain] = zero(sys)

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: LTI model.

parameters.name: gain
parameters.description: Zero-pole-gain form gain of the system.

tools.name: dcgain
tools.description: Compute the steady-state (zero-frequency) gain of a system, that is the final value of its step response. For discrete systems it evaluates the transfer function at z = 1. An infinite result signals a pure integrator in the loop.
tools.usage: k = dcgain(sys)

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: LTI model or array of models.

tools.name: damp
tools.description: Report the natural frequency, damping ratio and time constant of each pole of a system. Called with no output arguments it prints a formatted table of all poles. It is the quickest way to see which modes are slow, fast or poorly damped.
tools.usage:
damp(sys)
[wn, zeta] = damp(sys)
[wn, zeta, p] = damp(sys)

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: LTI model or a matrix (interpreted as an A matrix).

parameters.name: wn
parameters.description: Natural frequencies in rad/TimeUnit.

parameters.name: zeta
parameters.description: Damping ratios.

tools.name: bandwidth
tools.description: Compute the frequency at which the system gain first drops below a given level (by default -3 dB) relative to its DC gain. It is the standard single-number measure of closed-loop speed of response. Only meaningful for SISO systems with a finite DC gain.
tools.usage:
fb = bandwidth(sys)
fb = bandwidth(sys, dbdrop)

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: SISO LTI model.

parameters.name: dbdrop
parameters.description: Gain drop in dB defining the bandwidth (default -3).

tools.name: feedback
tools.description: Form the closed-loop interconnection of two systems in a feedback configuration. The default is negative feedback; pass +1 as the sign argument for positive feedback. Use feedback(L, 1) to get the closed-loop transfer function of a unity-feedback loop with open-loop L.
tools.usage:
sys = feedback(sys1, sys2)
sys = feedback(sys1, sys2, sign)
sys = feedback(sys1, sys2, feedin, feedout)
sys = feedback(sys1, sys2, feedin, feedout, sign)

parameters.name: sys1
parameters.description: Forward-path system.

parameters.name: sys2
parameters.description: Feedback-path system; use 1 for unity feedback.

parameters.name: sign
parameters.description: -1 for negative feedback (default) or +1 for positive.

parameters.name: feedin, feedout
parameters.description: Input and output indices of sys1 involved in the loop, for MIMO systems.

tools.name: series
tools.description: Connect two systems in series (cascade), optionally selecting which outputs of the first feed which inputs of the second. For SISO systems it is equivalent to the multiplication sys2*sys1, but the explicit index form is needed for MIMO connections. Note the ordering: series(sys1, sys2) means sys1 feeds sys2.
tools.usage:
sys = series(sys1, sys2)
sys = series(sys1, sys2, outputs1, inputs2)

parameters.name: sys1, sys2
parameters.description: Systems to cascade; sys1's output drives sys2's input.

parameters.name: outputs1, inputs2
parameters.description: Index vectors selecting which signals to connect for MIMO systems.

tools.name: parallel
tools.description: Connect two systems in parallel, so their outputs add for a shared input. For SISO systems this is the same as sys1 + sys2, but the index form supports partial MIMO connections. Use it to build models with multiple additive paths such as feedforward plus feedback.
tools.usage:
sys = parallel(sys1, sys2)
sys = parallel(sys1, sys2, inp1, inp2, out1, out2)

parameters.name: sys1, sys2
parameters.description: Systems whose responses are summed.

parameters.name: inp1, inp2
parameters.description: Input indices to be connected to the common input.

parameters.name: out1, out2
parameters.description: Output indices whose outputs are summed.

tools.name: connect
tools.description: Build a complex block-diagram model by connecting named subsystems through matching input and output signal names. You list the blocks and then the names of the overall inputs and outputs, and connect wires everything up automatically. It is far less error-prone than nesting series, parallel and feedback calls for multi-loop systems.
tools.usage:
sysc = connect(sys1, sys2, ..., inputs, outputs)
sysc = connect(sys1, ..., inputs, outputs, APs)
sysc = connect(blocks, connections, inputs, outputs)

parameters.name: sys1, sys2, ...
parameters.description: Models whose InputName and OutputName properties define the wiring; sumblk creates summing junctions.

parameters.name: inputs, outputs
parameters.description: Names of the signals that become the inputs and outputs of the assembled model.

parameters.name: APs
parameters.description: Analysis points to keep accessible for loop-opening analysis.

tools.name: c2d
tools.description: Convert a continuous-time model to discrete time at a given sample rate using zero-order hold, first-order hold, Tustin, impulse-invariant or matched methods. The choice of method affects fidelity, especially near Nyquist, and Tustin with prewarping preserves a chosen frequency exactly. This is the standard step before implementing a controller on a digital platform.
tools.usage:
sysd = c2d(sysc, Ts)
sysd = c2d(sysc, Ts, method)
sysd = c2d(sysc, Ts, opts)
[sysd, G] = c2d(___)

parameters.name: Ts
parameters.description: Sample time in seconds.

parameters.name: method
parameters.description: 'zoh' (default), 'foh', 'impulse', 'tustin', 'matched', 'least-squares'.

parameters.name: opts
parameters.description: c2dOptions with 'PrewarpFrequency', 'FractDelayApproxOrder'.

tools.notes: Choose Ts roughly 10 to 30 times faster than the closed-loop bandwidth.

tools.name: d2c
tools.description: Convert a discrete-time model back to continuous time using zero-order hold, Tustin or matched methods. Use it to analyse an identified discrete model in the continuous domain or to compare a digital controller against its analog prototype. Discrete models with poles at or near zero may have no exact continuous equivalent.
tools.usage:
sysc = d2c(sysd)
sysc = d2c(sysd, method)
sysc = d2c(sysd, opts)

parameters.name: method
parameters.description: 'zoh' (default), 'tustin', 'matched', 'least-squares'.

parameters.name: opts
parameters.description: d2cOptions with 'PrewarpFrequency'.

tools.name: minreal
tools.description: Compute a minimal realization by eliminating uncontrollable and unobservable states, and cancel near-coincident pole-zero pairs in transfer functions. Interconnecting models often creates redundant states that slow simulation and confuse analysis. The tolerance controls how close a pole and zero must be to be cancelled.
tools.usage:
sysr = minreal(sys)
sysr = minreal(sys, tol)
[sysr, U] = minreal(sys)

parameters.name: tol
parameters.description: Cancellation tolerance; default is based on the model's numerical conditioning.

parameters.name: U
parameters.description: Orthogonal state transformation used (state-space models only).

tools.name: balred
tools.description: Reduce the order of a model by balanced truncation, discarding states with small Hankel singular values that contribute little to the input-output behaviour. Use hsvd first to see how many states can safely be dropped. Essential for simplifying high-order FEM or identified models before control design.
tools.usage:
rsys = balred(sys, order)
rsys = balred(sys, orders, opts)
[rsys, info] = balred(___)
hsv = hsvd(sys)

parameters.name: order
parameters.description: Desired reduced order, or a vector of orders to compute several reductions.

parameters.name: opts
parameters.description: balredOptions with 'StateProjection' ('Truncate' or 'MatchDC'), 'FreqIntervals', 'Balancing'.

tools.name: ctrb
tools.description: Form the controllability matrix [B AB A^2B ... A^(n-1)B] of a state-space system. The system is controllable if this matrix has full rank, which is the condition for arbitrary pole placement. For numerically sensitive checks prefer ctrbf or the Gramian-based gram.
tools.usage:
Co = ctrb(A, B)
Co = ctrb(sys)

parameters.name: A, B
parameters.description: State and input matrices.

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: A state-space model, as an alternative to A and B.

tools.notes: rank(ctrb(...)) is numerically fragile for large systems; use ctrbf or hsvd instead.

tools.name: obsv
tools.description: Form the observability matrix [C; CA; CA^2; ...; CA^(n-1)] of a state-space system. Full rank means every state can be reconstructed from output measurements, which is the condition for observer design. It is the dual of controllability.
tools.usage:
Ob = obsv(A, C)
Ob = obsv(sys)

parameters.name: A, C
parameters.description: State and output matrices.

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: A state-space model.

tools.name: lqr
tools.description: Design a linear-quadratic regulator: the state-feedback gain K that minimizes the integral of x'Qx + u'Ru. It also returns the solution of the algebraic Riccati equation and the resulting closed-loop eigenvalues. Choosing Q and R by Bryson's rule (inverse squares of maximum acceptable values) is a good starting point.
tools.usage:
[K, S, P] = lqr(sys, Q, R)
[K, S, P] = lqr(sys, Q, R, N)
[K, S, P] = lqr(A, B, Q, R, N)

parameters.name: Q
parameters.description: State weighting matrix, positive semidefinite; larger penalizes state deviation more.

parameters.name: R
parameters.description: Control weighting matrix, positive definite; larger penalizes control effort more.

parameters.name: N
parameters.description: Optional cross-weighting term between states and inputs.

parameters.name: S, P
parameters.description: Riccati solution and closed-loop poles.

tools.notes: lqrd designs a discrete regulator for a continuous plant; dlqr works directly on discrete models.

tools.name: kalman
tools.description: Design a Kalman filter (state estimator) for a plant with process and measurement noise of given covariances. It returns the estimator as a state-space system, the optimal gain and the steady-state error covariance. Combine with lqr via lqgreg to build a full LQG controller.
tools.usage:
[kest, L, P] = kalman(sys, Qn, Rn)
[kest, L, P] = kalman(sys, Qn, Rn, Nn)
[kest, L, P] = kalman(sys, Qn, Rn, Nn, sensors, known)

parameters.name: sys
parameters.description: Plant augmented with noise inputs: ss(A, [B G], C, [D H]).

parameters.name: Qn
parameters.description: Process noise covariance.

parameters.name: Rn
parameters.description: Measurement noise covariance.

parameters.name: Nn
parameters.description: Cross-covariance between process and measurement noise.

parameters.name: sensors, known
parameters.description: Indices of measured outputs and known inputs.

tools.notes: For time-varying or nonlinear problems use the trackingKF, extendedKalmanFilter and unscentedKalmanFilter objects.

tools.name: place
tools.description: Compute a state-feedback gain matrix that places the closed-loop poles at specified locations, using a numerically robust algorithm that maximizes eigenvalue conditioning. For MIMO systems the extra freedom is used to improve robustness. Use it when you want to specify closed-loop dynamics directly rather than through LQR weights.
tools.usage:
K = place(A, B, p)
[K, prec] = place(A, B, p)

parameters.name: A, B
parameters.description: State and input matrices of the open-loop system.

parameters.name: p
parameters.description: Vector of desired closed-loop pole locations.

parameters.name: prec
parameters.description: Number of accurate decimal digits in the achieved poles.

tools.notes: place cannot handle pole multiplicity greater than rank(B); acker works for SISO systems but is numerically poor above about order 10.

tools.name: controlSystemDesigner
tools.description: Open the Control System Designer app for interactive SISO compensator design using root locus, Bode, Nichols and step-response views simultaneously. You drag poles and zeros or use automated tuning methods and see every response update live. Export the designed compensator to the workspace when finished.
tools.usage:
controlSystemDesigner
controlSystemDesigner(plant)
controlSystemDesigner(plant, comp)
controlSystemDesigner(views, plant, comp)
controlSystemDesigner('rlocus', plant)

parameters.name: plant
parameters.description: Plant model G.

parameters.name: comp
